cards.text: Last time, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, a man from the royal family, struck down Gedaliah, the governor the king of Babylon had appointed, and now the people are afraid of the Chaldeans (Jer 41:1-2, 18). So all the army commanders and all the people from the least to the greatest come to Jeremiah the prophet, along with Johanan son of Kareah, one of the army commanders (Jer 40:7-8), and Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, who comes right along with him. They ask Jeremiah to pray to the LORD for this remnant, because only a few of them are left.

cards.question: The commanders and the people want Jeremiah to pray for them. What do they want the LORD to tell them?

answers.text: The way to walk and what to do
How long Babylon will rule them
Who their next governor will be

cards.question: Jeremiah agrees to pray for the remnant, but says he'll only pass along the good news.

cards.text: Then the people make Jeremiah a promise, and they put the LORD Himself on the hook. They ask Him to be a true and faithful witness against them if they don't keep it.

cards.question: The people promise Jeremiah they'll obey the LORD's answer only if it's pleasant.

cards.text: After ten days, the word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah. TEN DAYS of everybody staring at those three little dots in the group chat!
Jeremiah calls together Johanan, the commanders and all the people, from the least to the greatest. Then he gives them the answer from the LORD, the God of Israel.

cards.question: The LORD's answer starts with an if. If the remnant does what, He'll build them up and not tear them down?

cards.text: Build up, not tear down. Plant, not uproot, and God even says He'll relent of the disaster He has brought on them.

cards.question: The LORD tells the remnant not to be ___ of the king of Babylon.
Why does the LORD say the remnant doesn't need to fear the king of Babylon?

answers.text: He is with them to save them
The king has gone back home
The king has made peace with them

cards.text: And it keeps getting BETTER. God says, "And I will show you compassion, and he will have compassion on you…"

cards.question: The LORD's promise to the remnant includes being restored to their own land.

cards.text: Staying in the land comes with all those promises. But then comes the second if: what if the remnant says, 'We will not stay in this land,' and disobeys the voice of the LORD?

cards.question: The LORD's second if pictures the remnant saying they'll go live in the land of ___ instead.
In the LORD's second if, what does the remnant say they won't face once they're living in Egypt?

cards.text: No war, no ram's horn, no hunger for bread. Egypt sounds like a travel ad with a palm tree on it, but now comes the word of the LORD for the remnant of Judah, if they're determined to go there and live.

cards.question: The remnant fears the sword and dreads the famine. If they go to Egypt, what does the LORD say the sword and famine will do?
The LORD says a few of those who go to live in Egypt will escape the disaster.

cards.text: Then God points back to Jerusalem. Just as His anger and wrath were poured out on the people living there, He says His wrath will be poured out on the remnant if they go to Egypt.

cards.question: If the remnant goes to Egypt, what does the LORD say they will never see again?

cards.text: Jeremiah makes it plain: "The LORD has told you, O remnant of Judah, 'Do not go to Egypt.' Know for sure that I have warned you today!"

cards.question: Jeremiah looks back at how the people sent him to pray and promised to do whatever the LORD said. He tells them they have ___ themselves.
Jeremiah tells the remnant they have obeyed the voice of the LORD in everything He sent him to tell them.
Where does Jeremiah say the remnant will die by sword and famine and plague?

answers.text: In the place they want to live
On the road back to Mizpah

cards.text: So the remnant has God's answer in their hands, and now they have to choose. Hang on, friend, because this story's not done yet.

findings.problem: Across 26 cards, Papa Dorin has only two real jokes: the group chat dots in stop 1 card 6 and the travel ad in stop 2 card 4. Most story cards are plain retelling with no reaction, disbelief or self-deprecation, even at moments that could hold a laugh. Examples are the people calling down the LORD as a witness against themselves (42:5), the promise of 'pleasant or unpleasant' (42:6), and Jeremiah telling them they deceived themselves (42:20). The voice reads like a pleasant narrator, not laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: The opening card stays within three sentences, but each sentence is a long run-on that packs in several clauses: Ishmael's lineage, Gedaliah's role, the fear of the Chaldeans, two cross-references, and 'Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, who comes right along with him,' which is filler. It carries far more than one beat and has none of Papa Dorin's voice. It reads as a dense block, not a bite-sized opener.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The story card quotes 42:12 and cuts it off with an ellipsis right before 'and restore you to your own land.' Card 13 then asks the baker whether the line goes on to promise restoration to their land. This sets the baker up to guess how a line they haven't seen finishes, instead of reasoning out its meaning.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The right answer 'This place' is two words in Bible wording and doesn't say what place it means. The wrong answers, 'The king of Babylon' and 'The prophet Jeremiah,' are longer and concrete. The right answer stands out by its length and its Bible phrasing, and without context it's also vague for the baker.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: 'Now they have to choose' implies the remnant hasn't decided yet. But in 42:20-21 Jeremiah says they have deceived themselves and 'have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God,' so the text presents their disobedience as already under way. The card also cites Jeremiah 42:22 but tells nothing from that verse.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The 'story's not over' line, 'Hang on, friend, because this story's not done yet,' nearly copies the doc's example line ('Trust me, friend, this story's not done.') instead of being a fresh line.

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.
